subject: About the latest article by Devlieger and Rosseel

messages.author: b5f242e7eb90c7c9
messages.subject: About the latest article by Devlieger and Rosseel
parts:
Dear all,

I have recently read the latest article by Devlieger and Rosseel in the journal Methodology, and it is an excellent article that discsused the use of Croon's approach to conduct factor score path analysis. At the end of the article, however, Devlieger and Rosseel states: 

'For the moment, the method of Croon also does not work for connected measurement models, such as models with cross-loadings or correlated residual errors.'

I am curious why the approach is inappropriate for models with cross-loadings? Any reference will be helpful!

Thanks,
Chester

messages.author: bfa43814f6ba1969
messages.subject: Re: About the latest article by Devlieger and Rosseel
parts:
Hi,

The Croon method is a variant of the classical correction for attenuation, which assumes that there errors are uncorrelated. There are extensions that allow for this, see:

Zimmerman, D. W. (2007). Correction for attenuation with biased reliability estimates and correlated errors in populations and samples. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 67(6), 920–939. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164406299132


Mikko

On 12/01/2017 09:01 AM, Chester Kam wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I have recently read the latest article by Devlieger and Rosseel in the
> journal Methodology, and it is an excellent article that discsused the
> use of Croon's approach to conduct factor score path analysis. At the
> end of the article, however, Devlieger and Rosseel states:
>
> 'For the moment, the method of Croon also does not work for connected
> measurement models, such as models with cross-loadings or correlated
> residual errors.'
>
> I am curious why the approach is inappropriate for models with
> cross-loadings? Any reference will be helpful!

The original idea was to create factor scores for each latent variable,
*one at a time*. Once the factor scores are computed, we apply Croon's
correction, followed by a path analysis using these factor scores as if
they were observed.

Of course, if you have cross-loadings, or correlated residuals across
latent variables, they will be ignored in this approach. One way out is
to extend the measurement model to include all 'connected' items, and
compute the factor scores for all latent variables involved
simultaneously. The best way to handle this is still under study.

Yves.
